title: Many-Shot CoT-ICL: Making In-Context Learning Truly Learn
claim: Prior view treats in-context examples as static retrieved patterns; ours treats them as an ordered curriculum enabling test-time learning.
layout: 2 panels, left-right split by dashed line, flow top-to-bottom, random-vs-ordered curve
description: A vertical dashed line splits the figure into two panels. Panel (a), "Traditional View: ICL as Static Retrieval & Pattern Matching", is a gray top-to-bottom flowchart. Training instances, drawn as grids of (Query, Answer) cards, feed an embedding model. Similarity retrieval then selects ICL demonstrations, which pass to a Generation box that maps Query x' to Output y'. Panel (b), "Proposed View: Many-Shot CoT as In-Context Test-Time Learning", uses green and teal. At the top is a curriculum sequence of Demo 1 to Demo n, each holding (Input, CoT, Output), linked by arrows. Below it are two green principle boxes: ease of understanding and smoothness of knowledge progression. At the bottom, a tangled orange scribble labeled Randomly Ordered CoT-ICL points by an arrow to a smooth green curve labeled Optimized Ordered CoT-ICL. This ordering step is called Curvilinear Demonstration Selection.
caption: Reframing of CoT-ICL as in-context test-time learning.
abstract: While many-shot ICL achieves remarkable performance, prior studies of its scaling behavior have mainly focused on non-reasoning tasks. In this work, we study many-shot ICL on reasoning tasks, with a particular focus on many-shot chain-of-thought in-context learning (CoT-ICL). Analyzing across non-reasoning and reasoning tasks and across non-reasoning and reasoning-oriented LLMs, we identify several distinctive properties of many-shot CoT-ICL. We further interpret these findings by viewing many-shot CoT-ICL as in-context test-time learning rather than scaled pattern matching, and suggest two principles: (i) demonstrations should be easy for the target model to understand, and (ii) they should be ordered to support a smooth conceptual progression. Guided by the principle, we propose Curvilinear Demonstration Selection (CDS), a simple ordering method that yields up to a 5.42 percentage-point gain on a math task with 64 demonstrations. Overall, our results reframe the long context window from a retrieval buffer into a structured curriculum for in-context test-time learning.
